To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ECM-infiltrating cells are more sensitive to PDT, and this sensitivity is independent of EMT.

1) ECM-infiltrating, chemoresistant pancreatic cancer cells exhibit increased sensitivity to photodynamic therapy, 2) ECM-infiltration promotes mesenchymal phenotypes and increased motility in 3D models of PDAC, 3) ECM rheology and matrix remodeling are important determinants of tumor cell motility, and 4) ECM-infiltrative cell populations exhibit increased chemosensitivity to photodynamic therapy.
pancreatic tumor cell subpopulations that are invasive and chemoresistant are sensitive to photodynamic therapy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the role of the extracellular matrix on pancreatic cancer cell behavior and response to therapy.
the role of ECM composition and rheology in regulating tumor cell behavior, and in particular, in determining responses to chemotherapies and to photodynamic therapy (Figure 1).
understanding the role of the extracellular matrix ( ECM ) in the regulation of pancreatic ductal aden carcinoma (PDAC) progression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this paper provides an integrative approach that is used to evaluate the invasive behavior and motile properties in rheologically characterized extracellular matrix as determinants of chemotherapeutics and photodynamic therapy responses.
the ECM-infiltrating, chemoresistant pancreatic cancer cell populations exhibit increased susceptibility to PDT.
this study provides evidence that the ECM composition and rheology regulate the growth, motility and response of pancreatic ductal adenacarcinoma to photodynamic therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that the most aggressive, ECM-invading, and chemoresistant populations of pancreatic ductal aden carcinoma cells exhibit increased sensitivity to photodynamic therapy.
we show that in 2D cultures, EMT does not confer sensitivity to PDT in the absence of matrix.

we show that in 2D cultures with ECM that promote invasive progression and in 3D models, response to PDT was markedly enhanced in the invasive populations, whereas the chemoresistant cells exhibited enhanced invasive potential.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ECM-infiltrating cells exhibit increased susceptibility to treatment with PDT in 3D models of pancreatic cancer.
the extracellular matrix can have profound effects on cancer cell behavior and that these effects are dependent on the specific properties of the matrix.
we can use the microenvironment to target the most aggressive, invasive, and chemoresistant populations of pancreatic cancer.
